questions.problem:
A function $g(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| $x$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $g(x)$ | $217$ | $234$ | $268$ | $336$ | $478$ |

Approximate ${g}^{′}(x)$ at the point $x=2$ using a backward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{g}^{′}(x)≈\frac{g(x)-g(x-h)}{h},
$$

 

at the point $x=2.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case, $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{g(2)-g(2-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{g(2)-g(1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{268-234}{1} \\  & =\frac{34}{1} \\  & =34.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The altitude $h(t)$ of a falling object object, measured in meters, is recorded every second for an interval of six seconds. The values of $h(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ | $5$ | $6$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $h(t)$ | $200$ | $195$ | $181$ | $159$ | $128$ | $91$ | $51$ |

Approximate the rate of change of the altitude when $t=3$ using a backward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{h}^{′}(t)≈\frac{h(t)-h(t-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the time $t=3.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{h}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{h(3)-h(3-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{h(3)-h(2)}{1} \\  & =\frac{159-181}{1} \\  & =-22.\end{aligned}
$$

So the rate of change of the altitude is $-22\,\text{m}/\text{s}.$

questions.problem:
The number of deer in a wildlife reserve, measured in hundreds, is given by the function $D(t)$, where $t$ is the time, in years, since the study began. The values of $D(t)$ for several values of $t$ are shown in the table below:

| $t$ | $0$ | $1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $4$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $D(t)$ | $5$ | $7$ | $10$ | $14$ | $19$ |

Approximate the rate of change of the deer population when $t=4$ using a backward difference approximation. Do not round the answer.

The estimated rate of change when $t=4$ is
{{field-1}} hundreds per year.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{D}^{′}(t)≈\frac{D(t)-D(t-h)}{h},
$$

at the time $t=4.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=1.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{′}(4) & ≈\frac{D(4)-D(4-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{D(4)-D(3)}{1} \\  & =\frac{19-14}{1} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the estimated rate of change when $t=4$ is $5$ hundreds per year.

questions.problem:
A baseball is hit by a batter. The distance between the batter and the ball, measured in miles, is given by the function $s(t)$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below:

| $t$ | $0$ | $0.5$ | $1$ | $1.5$ | $2$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $0$ | $0.015$ | $0.03$ | $0.045$ | $0.05$ |

Approximate the velocity ${s}^{′}(t)$ when $t=1$ using a backward difference approximation.
questions.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
{s}^{′}(t)≈\frac{s(t)-s(t-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the time $t=1.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(1) & ≈\frac{s(1)-s(1-0.5)}{0.5} \\  & =\frac{s(1)-s(0.5)}{0.5} \\  & =\frac{0.03-0.015}{0.5} \\  & =\frac{0.015}{0.5} \\  & =0.03.\end{aligned}
$$

So the velocity is $0.03\,\text{mi}/\text{s}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}{q}^{′}(2) & ≈\frac{q(2)-q(2-1)}{1} \\  & =\frac{q(2)-q(1)}{1} \\  & =186-192 \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}

A function $f(x)$ has values according to the table below:

| $x$ | $1$ | $4$ | $7$ | $10$ | $13$ | $16$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $-12$ | $-7$ | $-3$ | $7$ | $15$ | $21$ |

Approximate $f'(x)$ at the point $x=16$ using a backward difference approximation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
f'(x) \approx \frac{f(x) - f(x-h)}{h}
$$

 

at the point $x=16.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=3.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(16) & ≈\frac{f(16)-f(16-3)}{3} \\  & =\frac{f(16)-f(13)}{3} \\  & =\frac{21-15}{3} \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14058551/assets/6e3f77e5b7d491e3ee43c8f8150065282d2abc259e3a88751b93ff15b27f492a.png)

The graph of the function $g(x)$ is shown above. 
Approximate $g'(x)$ at the point $x=6$ using a backward difference approximation with step size $h=4.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
g'(x) \approx \frac{g(x) - g(x-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the point $x=6.$ Applying the above formula with $x=6$ and $h=4$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(6) & ≈\frac{g(6)-g(6-4)}{4} \\  & =\frac{g(6)-g(2)}{4} \\  & =\frac{6-4}{4} \\  & =\frac{2}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Estimating a Derivative Given a Table Using a Backward Difference Approximation: Word Problem
canonical_examples.problem:
A race car's position along a straight track, measured in meters from the starting line, is given by the function $s(t),$ where $t$ is the time in seconds. The values of $s(t)$ for different values of $t$ are given in the table below.

| $t$ | $1.2$ | $1.4$ | $1.6$ | $1.8$ | $2.0$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $s(t)$ | $1.3$ | $2.7$ | $2.9$ | $3.5$ | $5.0$ |

Approximate the velocity $s'(t)$ when $t=1.6$ using a backward difference approximation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
s'(t) \approx \frac{s(t) - s(t-h)}{h}
$$

 

at the time $t=1.6.$ We choose the step size $h$ to be as small as possible, in this case $h=0.2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{s}^{′}(1.6) & ≈\frac{s(1.6)-s(1.6-0.2)}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{s(1.6)-s(1.4)}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{2.9-2.7}{0.2} \\  & =\frac{0.2}{0.2} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So at the time $t=1.6,$ the velocity is approximately $1\, \textrm{m}/\textrm{s}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Estimating a Derivative Given a Graph Using a Backward Difference Approximation: Word Problem
canonical_examples.problem:
A factory produces fans. The total cost of producing $x$ fans, in dollars, is given by the function $C(x).$  The graph of $C(x)$ is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14058551/assets/ad3fae3694c4df8269be9a54350aabf83368b3152ea69eb2b9d1ac76e702823f.png)

Approximate the marginal cost $C'(x)$ at the point $x=3$ using a backward difference approximation with step size $h=2.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We use the backward difference approximation formula

$$
C'(x) \approx \dfrac{C(x) - C(x-h)}{h},
$$

 
at the point $x=3.$ Applying the above formula with $x=3$ and $h=2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}^{′}(3) & ≈\frac{C(3)-C(3-2)}{2} \\  & =\frac{C(3)-C(1)}{2} \\  & =\frac{30-20}{2} \\  & =\frac{10}{2} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

So the marginal cost is $\[math]5$ per fan.
